When the Sky Fell Over Grenada

Period 7 Sept – 25 Oct 2004
Location Mt. Moritz, St. George's
Written by Lennox Byron Campbell
a first-hand account

The Author

A life in service of the land and its people.

Lennox Byron Campbell is a Grenadian development consultant whose life's work has moved between board rooms, cocoa fields, and the communities where policy either arrives or doesn't. He has led institutions, lectured, chaired national agencies, and spent decades asking a single question: how does rural life in the Caribbean become more dignified, more productive, more just?

The journal you are about to read was written on scraps of paper, by candlelight, during the seven weeks after Hurricane Ivan flattened Grenada on 7 September 2004. Byron was a husband, father, manager, director — and for a few weeks, simply a man trying to keep his family safe and his community standing.

at home, Mt. Moritz

The Practitioner

For three decades, Byron built and ran the institutions that keep a small-island economy moving. He served as Secretary General of the Agency for Rural Transformation, then spent fifteen years as Manager of the Grenada Building & Loan Association — a position he held on the morning Ivan arrived and was still holding the afternoon the roof came off.

Later he would run the Marketing and Rural Enterprise Project and head the Rural Development Unit, always with the same orientation: projects are only as good as the farmers, makers, and young people they actually reach.

The Roles He Held

Byron has sat at the head of tables where small economies are negotiated — industry boards, regulatory bodies, consumer advocacy groups. He brought the same ear to each: listen first, speak carefully, move decisively.

  • 1984 – 1998 · Secretary General, Agency for Rural Transformation
  • 1998 – 2013 · Manager, Grenada Building & Loan Association
  • 1999 – 2001 · Chairman, Grenada Co-operative Nutmeg Association
  • 2008 – 2011 · Chairman, Marketing & National Importing Board
  • 1996 – 2013 · Director, Grenada Bureau of Standards
  • 2013 – 2018 · Project Manager, Marketing & Rural Enterprise Project
  • 2018 – 2023 · Head, Rural Development Unit

"A multi-disciplinary professional, passionate about people's development, the rule of law, and the participation of the youth to be the builders and leaders in the society."

— his own words

About the Journal

Written by candlelight, on scraps of paper.

For seven weeks beginning 7 September 2004, Byron wrote every night — mostly by candle, sometimes by a flashlight sent from family abroad, never with the comfort of a roof over his head. The house was open to the weather. His office was flooded. The government had effectively ceased to function. His wife, Gemma, his sons, his neighbours, his aging parents up in the mountain — everyone was improvising a life.

What follows is the journal exactly as it was written: a crisis in real time, with all its hunger and humour intact. It is a record of a family, a village, and a country improvising survival. It is also — quietly — a record of what dignity looks like when everything has been taken from you.

It was kept so that we should never forget to prepare for disasters of this nature in the future.

September 8, 2004

Before the Words, The Numbers

A category 3 storm, a nation remade in five hours.

Hurricane Ivan struck Grenada on the afternoon of 7 September 2004. Sustained winds of 120 mph, the eyewall passing directly over the island. The storm lasted from roughly 1:00 PM to 6:00 PM. By nightfall, an entire country had changed.

Across every parish. Roofs, walls, entire structures. Little distinction between rich homes and poor ones.

With an estimated 700 injured. The figure was lower than Hurricane Janet in 1955 — small comfort.

More than twice Grenada's annual GDP. About 45% of that total was housing alone.

On an island of roughly 102,000. One in six Grenadians had no home to return to.
0%

The national crop. Nutmeg takes seven years to bear fruit again. An entire industry gone overnight.
0/75

Only two of 75 public schools were left undamaged. An entire generation's education interrupted.
0 mph
sustained winds
Gusts peaking at 133 mph at Point Salines. The eyewall passed directly across the island.
0%

An economic event with no modern Caribbean parallel. Recovery would take more than a decade.

Ivan has made us equal. We are all the have-nots.

This is what happened, in his own words.

The Journal · Seven Weeks · Forty-Seven Entries

This journal was written by me over a seven week period. It began the day Hurricane Ivan devastated the Island of Grenada, killing 39 persons and injuring many, destroying 90% of the housing and almost all agriculture. The dislocation was so great that most institutions including government and police did not function for many days following the hurricane. The absence of security and inadequate planning and preparedness for hurricanes resulted in widespread looting. The entire State was paralyzed.

The entries are as they were entered at the time and record my family's responses and struggle during and after the hurricane. My family and I will ever be grateful to the Goddard family. Working as a unit we were able to overcome the difficulties which resulted from the hurricane. We are also extremely thankful to the many relatives and friends who gave us food and useful items to fight those trying days.

My wife, Gemma demonstrated the character fitting of a true heroine throughout the aftermath of the hurricane. This says a lot about the women of this country. All credit to them.

I dedicate this journal to my father, James Delcasse Campbell. I will forever remember his three words for living…
honesty · observation · psychology
Week One · The Storm

September 7, 2004

Tuesday Day of impact

We were at home monitoring the hurricane. The internet clearly showed that Ivan was going to have a direct hit on Grenada.

I was online with Kisha. Our preparations involved moving the potted plants indoors, relocating tables and securing the lawn chairs. Gemma secured the four dogs downstairs — Smigle, Flash, Noble and Spike. Smigle was wearing a cast on his broken leg. Fanon was anxious to experience a hurricane — this he would regret by 3:00 p.m. Hatuey and Royo were on the roof securing the galvanize with additional nails.

The wind began blowing at about 1:00 p.m. Soc and Royo were playing football in the playground — not the place to be at this time. Some time after 2:00 p.m. the wind speed increased to over 100 m.p.h. and soon afterwards there was a loud bang and off went the roof. Gemma screamed and called Hatuey from outside for us to go into the corridor; but since the roof over the corridor was already off, the next place in our exit plan was the laundry room downstairs.

Eric joined us about 3:45 p.m. He had seen our roof being blown away and had ventured down to our home, leaving his family behind, to look into our situation. By the time he arrived the wind speed had increased making it impossible for him to return. It was indeed a very courageous action.

We found ourselves in competition with the four dogs for limited space in a laundry room which was 8' × 12'. At one time I suggested to Gemma that we put the dogs in the rabbit hutch. She objected to this and soon afterwards the Celon mango tree crashed onto the rabbit hutch! Later into the evening when the wind had changed direction the mango tree was once more standing with the power of the wind. Indeed an amazing sight.

We saw the tower — a water tank encased in wood on our neighbour's house — disintegrate before our eyes in what appeared to be a tornado. Outside became white, visibility could not have been more than 10 feet. The wind was curling, making a long and humming sound and within two minutes the tower was gone. Fanon was beginning to appear sick — he wanted to lie down. He is asthmatic and his mother expressed her concern. He was heard saying that his life was changed forever.

At about 8:00 p.m. there was a break in the winds and we decided to leave the downstairs of our home. I must have fallen asleep about midnight next to Gemma on the floor, still hearing the howling of the wind from a hurricane that refused to go away after over 12 hours.

"Gemma said we have each other, we are all alive, let us be grateful. We hugged each other at the entrance of what used to be our home."

September 8, 2004

Wednesday Morning after

When morning came I could not believe what I saw. The village — Mt Moritz — was totally devastated.

All the buildings and trees were down. The earth was brown. I was in another place and time. Utility poles and cables were on the ground. It was total devastation. Gemma said we have each other, we are all alive, let us be grateful. We hugged each other at the entrance of what used to be our home. As I entered my yard and looked out onto the sea I saw two British battle ships coming into the harbour. I felt happy and sad, and cried. We were not alone.

By midday looting on a massive scale had begun in St. George's. I checked on Grenada Building & Loan building — my workplace. It was OK except for the roof. All the roof tiles were gone. Ms. Mc Leish, tenant in the building, was getting wet, but was adamant about staying there. Our offices had flooded but most of the equipment and files were covered and did not sustain any damage.

It was quite obvious that we had a major security problem on our hands. It appeared that the police had abandoned their post. All institutions were destroyed or rendered "out of order." There was no Government, no Church, and no Police. It was a "mess at best."

The situation facing us as a family demanded some type of military style living. We needed to be operating on maximum discipline given the conditions on the Island. My bag — worn on my back — became a permanent part of me. It contained my pistol, knife, flashlight, money, water, matches, notebook, pen, and sometimes energy food. Everyone was issued with flashlights and water. They were instructed on codes for raising alarms. They had to wear hard shoes at all times to avoid injuries. PRA training from the time of the revolution, I thought, was most instrumental.

September 10, 2004

Friday

Got up feeling hopeless, confused and overwhelmed by the task at hand.

I started many tasks at the same time. Gemma brought this to my attention — she is really a pillar of strength to the family. Dari came up to assist us with cleaning the house. Prepared rooms at Dona's house (unoccupied) for possible use.

First Community meeting at the SDA Church. Learned that there were 24 deaths in St. George's. Don't know what happened in the rest of the country. The community is attempting to cope with the crisis. There is, however, a problem of leadership and decision making.

My pickup truck got a punctured tyre — bottle — while I was trying to obtain water containers for the distribution of water. Soc and Greg at war; had to intervene. Was interviewed on T&T TV. Dinner was crackers and cheese, with lemon grass tea. Garvin brought us a battery charger — now we have cell phones — finally, communication!

I saw myself in a mirror for the first time since Ivan struck. Gemma wants me to shave, but so far I am resisting it.

September 11, 2004

Saturday

Left with Pauline, Soc and Titania to get water. Also obtained bleach and a stove from Ronald. Was able to repair damaged tyre at Baptist's on Cherry Hill. He is doing good business since there are so many punctures occurring due to nails and broken bottles. Went through the difficult process of sorting through hundreds of wet photos and drying them out in the sun.

We were visited by a doctor from the medical school. He was able to bring us up to date with international developments and coverage of Hurricane Ivan and the level of aid reaching Grenada — he had access to the internet. Ivan had now reached Jamaica (not a direct hit) and was now heading for Cuba — God bless them.

Hatuey is not pulling his weight. He did very little work today and we had a physical confrontation. I gave him a thump on his back. He left the house showing disrespect. The pressure of the crisis is causing tempers to rise.

I reflected as I thought about the day's events and the fact that Hatuey sustained the most personal loss among family members. His room was a total wreck. Most of his clothes, computer and belongings were either damaged or destroyed. He was preparing to begin university next year and maybe he was concerned about my ability to afford his education given the unknown future. I wondered how he was coping and maybe we all needed counseling to deal with the situation. But such help at this time was wishful thinking.

Towards evening Soc brought to my attention the condition of an English woman, Ms. Jones, who was on holiday when the hurricane struck and had lost everything — passport, clothes, medication, money. She was in bad shape. She is diabetic and had lost all her medication. She had to be rescued. Gemma shared her bed with her for the night. As for me I had to give up my bed and return to the doghouse for one more night.

September 12, 2004

Sunday

Another day of extreme heat. Up at 6:00 a.m. Decided that it would be wise to begin the outside clearing of debris. Ms. Jones was up. Gemma made her coffee and she had several calls from her family in the U.K. Gemma gave her a lovely black and white dress — I had bought this dress in the U.K. for Gemma when she was a size 9. Ms Jones looked beautiful. Gemma took her to the Airport where she was seen by a doctor and was cared for by British officials.

I had a talk with Hatuey. I told him that Ivan had changed life for all of us and his actions or words to me had a profound change in our relationship. He is now a man, he can leave if he wants, but to be realistic, we can do with his labour. We were all under tremendous pressure. He should understand that the situation will change. We needed to work and cooperate as a close unit to survive this disaster.

I heard this joke today. What are the similarities between a hurricane and a woman? Well, they both come wet and leave you without your house and your car.

Garvin called me from the mountain — Mt. Dor. He reported that the nutmeg field was a pasture — all nutmeg trees were grounded. They cascaded like a pack of dominoes. All cocoa, bananas — most trees — had fallen. I wondered how the old man, my father, would take this news. Up to two weeks before Ivan he had spoken to me about sub-dividing the property to his children. He is now 90 years old and I wish Ivan had not come in his lifetime. This will be very difficult for him.

I am sad that there would be no local fruits and food as we know it for a long time. So many things will change. My priorities will change. Never would I take many things for granted.

Week Two · Survival
Byron at home — some years later, the house rebuilt, the journal kept.

September 13, 2004

Monday

I had named Hurricane Ivan our "9/7."

Everyone had an early start. The boys, Gemma and Susie went to collect water at Tempe. I started with the cleaning of the garage and the front yard and steps. It was reported that Allan B. from Hubbard's had shot a looter. The situation is not good with Mr. Garnet and his family. His daughter is having a difficult time dealing with water and sanitation matters.

It is now almost one week since the Hurricane struck and I have made little progress with my roof. I am no carpenter and already I have busted my fingers using a hammer. The best news today is I was able to secure 2 tarpaulins. I now have 3 which should be adequate to cover my roof. I pray that the men show up tomorrow.

I had my first meeting with staff. The office was flooded. We can do nothing since there is no roof and electricity. We agree to meet again on Friday at 10:00 a.m.

September 14, 2004

Tuesday

An eventful day. It began with the fetching of water in Tempe. Saw the bread lines for the first time. We also were able to purchase fuel. I called Poui urging him to come home. I told him that his family and the community needed him, and that Pauline was both physically and mentally tired. I outlined the local conditions to him in clear language.

Gemma gave Buxo a good telling off. He made the mistake of raising the race issue. Little did he know that Gemma was waiting for him. She fixed him properly. He believes that he is white and black people are trash. The village got its first supply of relief goods — food and tarpaulin — today.

I heard the Prime Minister on radio for the first time. Poor leader, he is unable to talk to the people. Somehow he lacks the ability to be respected. He is not inspiring, not at all motivating.

September 15, 2004

Wednesday

A mixed day. We lost our 400 gallon water tank today along with 400 gallons of water. The platform was not level and it off-balanced. It was indeed another disaster for us. It took us many trips to Mt. Gay to fill the tank. Our plans to wash had to be abandoned.

Tempers remain high. Everyone is stressed. Hatuey and Fanon had serious words which were threatening to become physical. I had to intervene. I checked out the office. There was a light shower and within minutes water was pouring through. We cannot operate with a damaged roof.

Gemma needs help at home. She's having difficulties coping. (That is a lady of substance.) I got stung by a "mibone" — wasp — on my lip while having a glass of juice. Did not notice the damn insect in the glass.

The dogs were observed having fun! It is mating season.

September 17, 2004

Friday

A productive day.

Gemma finally got her wish to go to St. Andrew's. She reported that most of the trees in Birchgrove and Grand Etang had fallen. Damage to houses was not as severe compared to St. George's. Her family was doing O.K. The children went along for the drive.

Most of the day was spent at the office attempting to get all systems up and running for a limited period by next Monday. I requested security from the P.S., Finance. I also requested a tarpaulin from NERO. A case of diarrhea got the better of me while at the office. I was slow in lifting my shirt and low and behold the shit caught my shirt! Hatuey had to bring me clothing from home so I could leave the office.

We added a little more cover to our roof. We are now about 90% covered. We are living in a virtual tent.

· · · · ·

September 18, 2004

Saturday

My objectives for the day were to visit Mt. Do'r and to ensure that the GBLA had some kind of roof covering. Fanon and I made the trip to Mt. Do'r. Getting there was a 1½ hour trek up hill. It was a sad sight to see the entire nutmeg field on the ground.

There was a small cultural event in the village. Titania and I walked up to the road side event. In the quiet moonlight the drums echoed from Mount Merria. Pullet chanted "no woman no cry."

Water has finally arrived in good quantity. Our PVC pipe is serving a most important purpose. We now have pipe borne water. Gemma washed.

A mural of the island Byron has served all his life — the sea, the flame of the flamboyant tree, the hibiscus and heliconia of every Grenadian yard. The mural painted after Ivan, on a wall that had to be rebuilt.
Week Three · The Slow Turn Toward Order

September 19, 2004

Sunday

Poui came home today. His family was happy to see him. He came home with jerk chicken and Susie made a lovely dinner. I briefed Poui on developments within the village. I hope he takes on the leadership role. Soc started the chainsaw. We anticipate lots of work for this chainsaw. I tried the local mountain dew — it went down very smoothly with the moonlight.

Grenada — the country is not mobilized. As a people we are not. We are not even clearing our streets. Overseas soldiers are doing it for us. What are we doing! Where is the Government for God's sake?

Fanon and Royo are very excited about attending school in St. Vincent. With most of the school buildings damaged, many families are giving consideration to sending their children overseas. Gemma and I gave them a little talk on what is to be expected of them while there.

September 21, 2004

Tuesday

It is a beautiful half moon moving slowly towards the horizon, glittering as it shifts towards the soft Caribbean Sea. In the moonlight one cannot see the destruction of the land caused by Ivan.

This day was again a productive day. Checked Erick who was constructing a covering for a pit latrine. Pullet had some 15 buckets to move uphill. I did him the favour and dropped them for him. The other favour I did today was to get a tarpaulin for Pilton. Had to go through NERO and Point Salines.

Terry started on my temporary roof. His team is doing a fine job, but it was sad to see the demise of Soc's famous bucket support system. Erick gave good support in moving and clearing the fallen trees in the yard.

Roseman and his wife both passed away. To some degree it all had to do with Ivan.

September 22, 2004

Wednesday

I was depressed today after a drive through the rain forest — Grand Etang. All the trees are gone. My concern is for the ecology and what would happen when the heavy rains come. Would it bring landslides?

Terry completed the roof. He did a good job — to be tested when the rains arrive. It is over two weeks since we had rain of any consequence. Pilton got his tarpaulin today and Terry should set him up tomorrow.

The boys — Fanon and Royo — confirmed to attend school in St. Vincent. They are booked to travel on Friday. There is talk about a Government of Reconstruction comprising the Government and the Opposition. We shall see what develops from this.

Weeks Four to Seven · Rebuilding

September 25 – 26, 2004

Saturday – Sunday

The boys left today for St. Vincent. Gemma took them to the airport. Their "Church clothes" were all packed. They were excited about a temporary new life in St. Vincent. Reggie said that Fanon pointed out his Church clothes on arrival.

Community work was held today, it was well supported. However we had only two trucks. I gave 2½ hours. The Red Cross delivered two truck loads of food. Their system of distribution did not work out as planned. People complained about their names not being on the list and we were not at our best behaviour.

The radio and lights sent by Kisha and Kent are truly making a difference. We are very thankful.

October 1, 2004

Friday

Emotionally, a better day compared to the day before. The reality of the effects and implications of the hurricane is only now coming to the fore. Garvin was laid off today with two weeks' pay — not good news. Also today, bandits hit St. George's — masked armed men. GCNA's truck had a serious accident — 5 hospitalized.

Our street, Church Street, has seen the loss of 20 persons. From a total population of 33 persons only 13 remain. I am looking forward to the day when they would all be back.

October 4, 2004

Monday

I had a chat with Einstein about his experience during the hurricane. From his account, he did some very heroic things. He went out during the hurricane to rescue Mr. Lennie. He entered the house during the fury of the storm to remove both husband and wife. He also told me about the strange wave that almost took the lives of himself, Yellow Boy and Alister while they were diving at Point Salines.

A busy day at the office. I will be having a meeting with the adjusters on Wednesday. I hope it will be a favourable encounter. I will consider $200,000 settlement a God send — the cost of restoration has been estimated at $256,000.

More tarpaulins are appearing on buildings day by day. The noises of generators are filling the night as more villagers take steps to provide electricity for their homes. It is obvious that electricity would take months to arrive at Mt. Moritz. It is one month now since Ivan and one cannot feel the presence of the Government.

October 5 – 6, 2004

Tuesday – Wednesday A reprieve

God did bless me. I received a fair settlement from the Insurance Company, Cunningham and Lindsey.

Neal, the Agent was very reasonable. Gemma and I are pleased with the final settlement. We have begun to discuss options re restoration of our home. We also obtained a 45KV generator ($3,000) from the U.K. Hopefully, by tomorrow, we shall have electricity. I wore my T-shirt, "All hands on deck to rebuild our country." Tomorrow I shall wear "Stand up Grenada."

Colin Powell visited the Spice Isle today. It is very uncertain what will emerge from the visit. So far the U.S. contribution to the Island has been negligible. The nutmeg industry is in a tail spin. Hundreds of workers are likely to be affected.

October 8, 2004

Sunday The mountain

Up early and prepared for the mountain. Picked up Orgas and Garvin at Moliniere. I then proceeded to Brooklyn to take up Vibert, Lesley and Edwin. Our task was to clear the road and attempt to drive up the mountain — Mt. Do'r. We got stuck in soft mud left from a landslide. It took lots of manpower to push the vehicle out of the mud.

We made our way up the mountain and again, looking at the plantation, it was a total disaster; an entire lifetime of cultivation and hard work gone in the twinkle of an eye.

There is no way my father can face this. It will kill him. At 90 years old he, James D. Campbell, could not handle this. Having been born in the mountain and educated by his father who was a school principal, James went on to be the Assistant Manager of Geest Industries and to be one of Grenada's best farmers. He was, for many years, the country's Farmer of the Year. His plantation was the most diversified farm on the entire Island. He would be quick to tell you, however, that his success had all to do with his most precious wife, Pearl.

The evidence of the prickly fibrous roots of the nutmeg trees was now exposed. Ivan had absolutely no problem uprooting those huge trees. They lie on the ground like domino cards — dying. I have the profound memory of days gone by when you could walk through that forest of trees and wonder at the sound — yes, the sound of the trees, the smell of the nutmegs and the wonder of it all.

It was a smack reminder of life. We should not take anything for granted. Live every day to the fullest. Every moment is precious. If only I could see those wonderful trees just for a moment. I have the memory.

October 13 – 14, 2004

Wednesday – Thursday

My birthday was yesterday, the 13th. It was uneventful save for the fact that Gemma and I had lunch at Creole Shack. Kisha and Kent called. It was a happy moment. Gemma and I are having the usual morning walk — 5:00 to 6:00. However, I can sense her tension and stress from the post Ivan reality. She has been a tower of strength for all.

Today the Insurance Company paid up. Now we can pursue the restoration of our home. I am uncertain at this time of the right moment to do so. This would depend on finding the right builder who is available and affordable.

October 15 – 17, 2004

Friday – Sunday

Saturday Gemma and I made a round-the-Island tour. Our first stop was at the Grenville market. We were not very impressed with the quantity and quality of vegetables available. However, we did do some purchases. Next we visited Ie. She was glad to see us and was in good spirits. Then it was on to Aunty Claris and Cyo. We had breakfast and a long chat. We talked about politics, economic and social issues.

Mr. Chase, in writing in the Grenada Informer newspaper, said, "the Lord gave me the nutmeg trees and now he has taketh all away — thank you Lord."

Sunday was our first drive to Mt. Do'r. Garvin and the men gave me a good help in cutting and clearing damaged trees through the citrus orchard. I was totally burnt out by 12:30 p.m. We accomplished quite a lot. Gemma made "titirey" fishcake and a nice salt fish souse with provisions for lunch.

I love my woman — in all ways.

October 23 – 25, 2004

Saturday – Monday Final entries

The boys — Fanon and Royo — are home for a few days. Their school in St. Vincent was closed for the week. Dwayne accompanied them. Gemma was pleased to see and have her son. She said that she missed cooking for him. We went to the beach — lots of fun.

There was plenty of traffic pertaining to the building of the kitchen. Robert is my choice for cabinet maker. We have decided to contract Carl John to repair our home and I am planning to go to T&T to purchase building material. The cleaning up in the village continued. I was unable to participate due to a toothache. The Prime Minister had his first meeting in Mt. Moritz and promised everything — housing, etc.

To date we have no telephone and electricity. However, we do have water, hope and lots of love from each other.

❦

Today I will end this journal. As I end, Grenada is in a sad state of affairs. The task seems overwhelming. The environment, lives, houses, trees, the economy and the State are all in shambles.

But we WILL make it right. We are a determined people. Time will tell.

— Byron, 25 October 2004

A record kept so we do not forget.

Byron rebuilt his home. His sons finished school. Grenada rebuilt — slower, more carefully. The nutmeg industry took most of a decade to recover. This journal, kept on scraps of paper by candlelight, is one family's first-hand account of what it costs when a category 3 hurricane passes directly over a small island, and what it takes to carry on afterward.

Colophon
